questions.question: What is a race condition and how do you identify one in code?
questions.title: Race Condition Identification in Java
questions.direct_answer: A race condition is a bug where the program's output depends on the timing of thread execution. It occurs when multiple threads access shared mutable state without synchronization. Look for: shared mutable fields accessed from multiple threads without synchronized, volatile, or AtomicX.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can spot race conditions in code — practical skill for production debugging
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only describing race conditions abstractly — not being able to point to one in actual code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the exact code pattern that causes a race condition and explain the specific interleaving that breaks it

sections.title: Understanding Race Conditions in Concurrent Java
sections.content:
A **race condition** is a bug where the program's result depends on the order in which threads run. Two threads touch the same data at the same time, and the final value depends on who finishes last.

This happens when threads share **mutable state** without a lock. Even one line like `counter++` is really three steps under the hood: read the value, add one, write it back. The **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine) can pause a thread between any two of those steps and let another thread run.

> **Key rule:** if a non-final field is read and written by more than one thread with no `synchronized`, `volatile`, or `AtomicInteger`, you probably have a race condition.

In production these bugs are **non-deterministic**. They pass every single-threaded test, then fail at random under load — wrong counts, missing rows, and state you cannot reproduce on your laptop.

sections.title: How an Interleaving Loses an Update
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Thread A reads count = 10] --> B[Thread A adds one
in a register] A2[Thread B reads count = 10] --> C2[Thread B writes 11] B --> C[Thread A writes 11] C2 --> D{Both wrote
the same 11?} C --> D D -- Yes --> E[One increment is lost] ```

sections.content:

emerald|Symptoms|~Hard to reproduce|works in dev|fails under load|flaky tests

sections.title: Wrong: an unsynchronized counter loses updates
Right: AtomicInteger makes each increment atomic
When Race Conditions Occur
sections.content:
Race conditions occur when you have **shared mutable state** accessed by multiple threads without synchronization. Common spots in a Java backend: a counter tracking requests across servlet threads, a cache map updated by concurrent API calls, or a status flag checked and changed by different workers.

You will see them most in Spring `@Service` singletons where instance fields are shared across request threads. Any time a non-final field in a singleton bean gets modified, ask: **can two threads reach this at once?** If yes, and there is no `synchronized`, `volatile`, or `AtomicX`, you have likely found a race condition waiting to happen.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming single statements are atomic**: freshers think `counter++` or `list.add()` is safe because it is one line of Java, not realizing it compiles to several bytecode instructions that can interleave.
- **Synchronizing only the getter**: adding `synchronized` to `getCount()` but not to `incrementCount()` does not help — both the read and the write need the same lock.
- **Testing on a single core**: a race may stay hidden on a single-core container, then appear in production on multi-core servers where true parallelism happens.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Race condition**: a bug where correctness depends on thread timing — the output changes based on which thread runs first.
- **Shared mutable state**: the root cause — multiple threads reading and writing the same modifiable variable.
- **Non-atomic operations**: even `counter++` is three steps (read-modify-write) that can interleave at the bytecode level.
- **Identification pattern**: non-final instance fields in shared classes with no `synchronized`, `volatile`, or `AtomicX` protection.
- **AtomicInteger**: lock-free atomic updates on numeric counters using a CPU compare-and-swap.
- **Non-deterministic failures**: the bug appears at random under load, which is exactly why it is hard to reproduce.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A race condition is when your program's correctness depends on the timing of thread execution. It happens when multiple threads access shared mutable data without proper synchronization. Let me show you a concrete example. Say you've got a request counter in a Spring service that's tracking API calls. The counter field is just an int, and every request thread calls increment on it. Now here's the problem: even though counter-plus-plus looks like one operation, it's actually three at the bytecode level — read the current value, add one, write it back. Thread A reads ten, gets paused by the scheduler before writing, then Thread B also reads ten, increments to eleven, and writes. Thread A resumes and also writes eleven. You've lost one increment. That's a race condition. To identify them in code, I look for non-final instance fields in singleton beans that get modified. If there's no synchronized keyword, no volatile, and it's not an AtomicInteger, that's a red flag. The tricky part is these bugs don't always show up in testing. They appear randomly under load when true parallelism kicks in. The fix is either using AtomicInteger for counters, or wrapping the operation in a synchronized block so only one thread can execute it at a time.

The scheduler can pause any thread mid-step. A line like `count++` isn't one action. It's a read, then an add, then a write. In that gap, another thread reads the old value too. So both threads write back the same number.

questions.question: What is starvation in multithreading?
questions.title: Thread Starvation in Java
questions.direct_answer: Thread starvation occurs when a thread is perpetually denied access to a resource because higher-priority threads or other threads keep getting scheduled first. The thread is alive and ready but never gets CPU time or the lock it needs to make progress.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the three main concurrency problems: race conditions, deadlock, and starvation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing starvation with deadlock — in starvation the thread could eventually run; in deadlock it never can
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete cause like always using notify instead of notifyAll when there are multiple waiters

sections.title: Understanding Thread Starvation
sections.content:
**Thread starvation** is when a thread is ready to run but never gets its turn. It stays alive and waiting while other threads keep getting picked ahead of it.

Think of waiting in line while the barista keeps serving people who arrived after you. You are not stuck forever in theory — you just never reach the front. That is the difference from deadlock: a starved thread *could* run, it just never does.

In Java, starvation has a few common causes. **Thread priorities**: if high-priority threads keep running, low-priority ones may never get CPU time. **Unfair locks**: the same thread keeps re-acquiring a lock before waiting threads get a turn. **`notify()` instead of `notifyAll()`**: `notify()` wakes only one thread, and the JVM might wake the same one every time.

> **Key rule:** the JVM scheduler is **not** guaranteed to be fair. If fairness matters, you must enforce it with a fair `ReentrantLock`.

sections.title: Why a Waiting Thread Never Gets Picked
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S[Scheduler picks next thread] --> H[High-priority thread runs] H --> S S -. never picked .-> L[Low-priority thread
ready but waiting forever] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Starvation|~Denied resource|never gets CPU/lock|others keep winning|no progress
blue|Causes|~Unfairness|greedy high-priority|always-held locks|biased scheduling
emerald|Fairness|~The remedy|fair ReentrantLock|fair Semaphore|round-robin

sections.title: Wrong: notify() can leave most workers starving
Right: notifyAll() plus a fair lock prevent starvation
When Starvation Occurs
sections.content:
Starvation shows up wherever there is **resource contention and unfair allocation**. In thread pools, some tasks keep getting picked while others wait indefinitely. In producer-consumer code, using `notify()` with several consumers can leave some of them asleep forever.

Lock starvation happens with the default (unfair) `ReentrantLock` when one thread keeps re-acquiring under heavy contention. Database connection pools can starve threads if connections are not released fairly. The tell-tale sign: some threads make progress while others **with the same priority** stay blocked despite being ready to run.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing starvation with deadlock**: in deadlock, threads can never proceed; in starvation, a thread *could* run but keeps getting deprioritized.
- **Using `notify()` instead of `notifyAll()`**: the classic cause — freshers think `notify()` is more efficient, not realizing it can leave threads starving.
- **Assuming the JVM scheduler is fair**: same-priority threads may not get equal time, so you need an explicit fair `ReentrantLock` for FIFO ordering.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Starvation**: a thread is perpetually denied resources despite being ready — not blocked, just never scheduled.
- **Thread priorities**: low-priority threads can starve under constant high-priority load — the scheduler is not guaranteed fair.
- **notify vs notifyAll**: `notify()` with many waiters can wake the same thread repeatedly, starving the rest.
- **Unfair locks**: the default `ReentrantLock` is unfair, so the same thread can keep winning the lock.
- **Fair locks**: `new ReentrantLock(true)` guarantees FIFO ordering and prevents lock starvation.
- **Different from deadlock**: a starved thread could eventually run; a deadlocked one never can.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Thread starvation is when a thread is perpetually denied the resources it needs to run. It's alive, it's ready, but the scheduler or resource allocation keeps giving priority to other threads, so it never gets its turn. The key difference from deadlock: in starvation, the thread could theoretically run eventually, it's just being continuously passed over. In deadlock, the thread can never proceed under any circumstance. A concrete example is using notify instead of notifyAll. Say you've got a producer-consumer queue with five worker threads all waiting for tasks. When a task arrives, you call notify, which wakes only one thread. The problem is the JVM might always pick the same thread to wake. The other four threads just sit there, starving. The fix is notifyAll, which wakes all waiting threads and lets them compete fairly. Another cause is thread priorities. If you have high-priority threads that keep running, low-priority threads might never get CPU time. The JVM scheduler isn't guaranteed to be fair. With locks, the default ReentrantLock is unfair, meaning threads don't acquire in first-come-first-served order. You can fix this by creating a fair lock with the fairness parameter set to true, which guarantees FIFO ordering. The takeaway: starvation is about unfair resource allocation, not threads being stuck.

questions.question: What is thread interference and how does it cause problems?
questions.title: Thread Interference in Java
questions.direct_answer: Thread interference occurs when operations from different threads interleave on shared mutable data, producing incorrect results. Even simple operations like counter-plus-plus can interleave at the bytecode level because they compile to multiple instructions: read, add, write. This causes lost updates.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deeper understanding of how operations interleave at the CPU and bytecode level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming single-statement Java code is always atomic — not knowing that counter-plus-plus is three operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the exact bytecode-level interleaving that causes a lost update in a counter increment

sections.title: Thread Interference at the Bytecode Level
sections.content:
**Thread interference** is when steps from different threads mix together on the same shared data and produce a wrong result.

The core idea: a single Java statement is not always atomic. When you write `counter++`, the compiler turns it into three bytecode instructions — load the value, increment it, store it back. The **JVM** scheduler can pause a thread between any two of those instructions and let another thread run its own read-modify-write.

That creates the **lost update problem**. Two threads both increment a counter that starts at ten. Thread A reads ten and pauses. Thread B reads ten, writes eleven. Thread A resumes and also writes eleven. The final value is eleven, not twelve — one increment is gone.

> **Key rule:** the scheduler switches at the **bytecode instruction** boundary, not at the Java line boundary. So "one line" tells you nothing about safety — only `synchronized` or an `AtomicInteger` makes the whole read-modify-write indivisible.

sections.title: The Interleaving That Loses an Update
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Thread A
    participant M as Shared count
    participant B as Thread B
    A->>M: read count (10)
    Note over A: computes 11, not stored yet
    B->>M: read count (10)
    B->>M: write 11
    A->>M: write 11
    Note over M: final value 11, one update lost
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Thread Interference|~Interleaved steps|two threads, shared data|operations overlap|corrupted result
blue|Read-Modify-Write|~Not atomic|count++ is 3 steps|interleave between them|lost update
emerald|Where|~Shared mutable fields|counters, collections|instance state|static state
violet|Fixes|~Serialize or isolate|synchronized|atomics|ThreadLocal

sections.title: Wrong: count++ interleaves across threads
Right: AtomicInteger does the whole step atomically
When Thread Interference Happens
sections.content:
Thread interference happens whenever multiple threads run **non-atomic operations on shared mutable state**. It is common in counters and statistics across servlet threads — page views, API call counts, error tallies.

Any compound operation is vulnerable: check-then-act (`if (count > 0) count--`), read-modify-write (`balance += amount`), or pairs that look atomic but are not (`list.size()` then `list.add()`). The JVM only guarantees atomic reads and writes of primitives (except `long` and `double` on 32-bit JVMs) and reference assignments. For everything else, use `synchronized`, an `AtomicX` class, or `volatile` for visibility only.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming single statements are atomic**: the biggest mistake — thinking `counter++` is safe because it is one line, not realizing the bytecode has several instructions.
- **Synchronizing only one side**: adding `synchronized` to the getter but not the increment does not prevent interference — both need the same lock.
- **Thinking `volatile` fixes interference**: `volatile` ensures visibility but does **not** make compound operations atomic — `volatile int` with `count++` still loses updates.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Thread interference**: interleaving of non-atomic operations on shared data, causing wrong results like lost updates.
- **Non-atomic operations**: `counter++` compiles to multiple bytecode instructions (read, modify, write).
- **Lost update**: two increments produce only one net change because the writes overwrite each other.
- **Bytecode level**: the scheduler can switch between any two bytecode instructions, not just Java statements.
- **AtomicInteger**: uses CPU compare-and-swap to perform the increment as one atomic hardware step.
- **volatile is not enough**: it guarantees visibility, not atomicity — use `AtomicX` or `synchronized` for compound operations.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Thread interference is when operations from different threads interleave on shared data in a way that produces wrong results. The key point here is that even a single line of Java code isn't necessarily atomic. Take counter-plus-plus. You write one statement, but the compiler turns that into three bytecode instructions: load the current value from memory, add one, store the result back. Now here's where interference happens. Thread A loads ten, calculates eleven, but before it can store, the JVM scheduler pauses it and switches to Thread B. Thread B also loads ten — because A hasn't written yet — calculates eleven, and stores eleven. Thread A resumes and stores its eleven, overwriting B's update. Final result is eleven instead of twelve. One increment was lost. That's the lost update problem. Freshers often assume single Java statements are atomic because they're one line of code. That's the mistake. The JVM can context-switch between any bytecode instruction. To fix this, you use AtomicInteger, which uses a compare-and-swap CPU instruction to do the entire increment atomically. Or you use a synchronized block so only one thread executes the read-modify-write at a time. Volatile doesn't help here because it only guarantees visibility, not atomicity of compound operations.

questions.question: What is deadlock and what are the four conditions required for it?
questions.title: Deadlock Four Conditions in Java
questions.direct_answer: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion (resources are non-shareable), Hold and Wait (holding one resource while waiting for another), No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and Circular Wait (circular chain of waiting threads). Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the formal deadlock conditions — often asked in senior or strong fresher interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing deadlock only as two threads waiting for each other without naming the four Coffman conditions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all four Coffman conditions and explain which one is easiest to break in Java code — typically Circular Wait through lock ordering

sections.title: Deadlock and the Four Coffman Conditions
sections.content:
**Deadlock** is when two or more threads are stuck forever, each holding a lock the other needs.

Think of two cars meeting on a one-lane bridge — neither can pass, and neither will reverse. Computer scientist Edward Coffman listed four conditions that must **all** be true at the same time for deadlock to happen, called the **Coffman conditions**: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait.

The powerful part is that you only need to break **one** of them to make deadlock impossible.

> **Key rule:** in Java code, the easiest condition to break is **Circular Wait** — acquire your `synchronized` locks in one consistent global order (say, by ascending `id`) so a cycle can never form.

The classic Java case: Thread A locks Resource 1 then waits for Resource 2, while Thread B locks Resource 2 then waits for Resource 1. Both wait forever.

sections.title: The Circular Wait That Forms a Deadlock
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR T1[Thread 1
holds Lock A] -->|waits for| LB[Lock B] T2[Thread 2
holds Lock B] -->|waits for| LA[Lock A] LB --> T2 LA --> T1 ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Mutual Exclusion|~Coffman 1|resource non-shareable|one holder at a time|the lock itself
blue|Hold and Wait|~Coffman 2|holds one lock|waits for another|grabs incrementally
emerald|No Preemption|~Coffman 3|cannot force-release|holder keeps it|until done
violet|Circular Wait|~Coffman 4|A waits B, B waits A|the cycle|break this one to prevent

sections.title: Wrong: lock order depends on the arguments
Right: always lock the lower id first
When Deadlock Prevention Matters
sections.content:
You need to prevent deadlock any time your code acquires **more than one lock**. This is critical in fund transfers between accounts (each account is a lock), inventory updates across multiple products, or database code that locks multiple rows.

In Spring `@Transactional` methods that call other services, inconsistent lock orders can deadlock at the database level too. The most practical fix is **lock ordering** — always acquire locks in the same global order, such as by ascending ID. As a safety net, use `tryLock` with a timeout from `ReentrantLock` so a thread can give up instead of waiting forever.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only describing two threads waiting**: saying "A waits for B and B waits for A" without naming the four Coffman conditions loses points in formal interviews.
- **Thinking `synchronized` alone prevents deadlock**: it prevents race conditions, but inconsistent lock order with `synchronized` is exactly what *causes* deadlock.
- **Not knowing which condition to break**: in Java, breaking Circular Wait via lock ordering is the standard solution — many freshers do not know this.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deadlock**: permanent blocking where threads wait in a cycle for locks held by each other.
- **Mutual Exclusion**: a lock can only be held by one thread at a time.
- **Hold and Wait**: a thread holds one lock while waiting to acquire another.
- **No Preemption**: a lock cannot be forcibly taken — the holder must release it.
- **Circular Wait**: a closed chain of threads each waiting on the next thread's lock.
- **Prevention**: break any one condition — lock ordering breaks Circular Wait and is the most practical in Java.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Deadlock is when two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource the other holds. For deadlock to happen, you need all four Coffman conditions present at the same time. Let me name them. First, Mutual Exclusion — the resource can't be shared, like a synchronized lock that only one thread can hold. Second, Hold and Wait — a thread holds one lock while trying to acquire another. Third, No Preemption — you can't forcibly take a lock away, it has to be released voluntarily. Fourth, Circular Wait — there's a circular chain where thread A waits for thread B's lock, and B waits for A's lock. Here's the key insight: you only need to break one condition to prevent deadlock. In Java code, the easiest one to break is Circular Wait by using lock ordering. That means if you need to lock two accounts, always lock them in ascending ID order. Thread one locks account ten then account twenty. Thread two also locks ten then twenty. Now there's no cycle, no deadlock. Some freshers think synchronized alone prevents deadlock, but that's wrong — deadlock happens when you have multiple synchronized blocks acquired in inconsistent order. The interviewer is testing whether you know the formal conditions, not just the intuitive explanation.

questions.question: What is livelock and how is it different from deadlock?
questions.title: Livelock vs Deadlock in Java
questions.direct_answer: In deadlock, threads are blocked and do nothing. In livelock, threads are actively running but making no progress — they keep responding to each other's actions but never proceed. Both result in the system being stuck, but livelock burns CPU while deadlock does not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Distinguishing between the two types of stuck conditions — deadlock versus livelock
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing livelock with deadlock or not having a concrete example of livelock
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the classic polite people in a hallway analogy and explain why livelock is harder to detect in production

sections.title: Deadlock vs Livelock: Different Ways to Get Stuck
sections.content:
**Deadlock** and **livelock** both mean the system stops making progress, but they behave very differently.

In **deadlock**, threads are blocked, parked, and waiting for a lock. They use almost no CPU and sit in the `BLOCKED` state. In **livelock**, threads keep running and executing code, but they react to each other endlessly without ever finishing.

The classic picture: two polite people meet in a narrow hallway. Both step right to let the other pass, blocking again. Both step left, blocking again. They keep moving but never get through.

In code, livelock usually comes from optimistic retry logic. Imagine two threads that each grab one lock with `tryLock`, fail to get the second, politely release the first, and retry — in perfect lockstep. They collide on every attempt, so neither ever proceeds even though both are busy spinning. The fix is to break the symmetry: add randomized backoff so the threads retry at different moments, or impose a consistent lock order.

> **The gotcha:** livelock is harder to spot than deadlock — a thread dump from `jstack` shows the threads as `RUNNABLE`, so monitoring thinks everything is fine while CPU burns and nothing advances.

sections.title: The Retry Loop That Never Resolves
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Thread grabs first lock] --> B[Tries second lock] B --> C{Got it?} C -- No --> D[Release first lock
and retry] D --> A C -- Yes --> E[Make progress] ```

sections.title: Deadlock vs Livelock Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Deadlock | Livelock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thread state | BLOCKED or WAITING | RUNNABLE (actively executing) |
| CPU usage | Zero — threads parked | High — threads spinning |
| Progress | No progress, waiting forever | No progress, but actively trying |
| Detection | Thread dumps show BLOCKED | Hard to detect, appears busy |
| Typical cause | Circular lock acquisition | Collision detection and retry |

sections.title: Livelock: Active but Making No Progress
When Each Problem Occurs
sections.content:
**Deadlock** occurs when acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order — the classic case is two account transfers locking in opposite directions. You will see threads stuck in `BLOCKED` state waiting for synchronized locks or database row locks.

**Livelock** occurs in optimistic retry scenarios where threads detect a conflict and back off, but their retry timing keeps colliding. It is common in lock-free algorithms using compare-and-swap where many threads repeatedly fail the swap and retry. In production, use `jstack` or thread dumps to tell them apart: deadlock shows `BLOCKED` threads with clear lock dependencies, while livelock shows `RUNNABLE` threads with high CPU and no progress.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using the terms interchangeably**: calling every stuck condition "deadlock" misses that livelock is a distinct problem with different symptoms.
- **Not knowing the hallway analogy**: it is the standard explanation interviewers expect — not having it ready looks unprepared.
- **Forgetting CPU usage**: the key differentiator is that livelock burns CPU while deadlock does not — leaving this out misses the practical impact.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deadlock**: threads permanently blocked on each other — zero CPU, threads in `BLOCKED` state.
- **Livelock**: threads actively running but making no progress — high CPU, threads in `RUNNABLE` state.
- **Hallway analogy**: two people keep stepping the same way, blocking each other again and again.
- **Detection difference**: deadlock shows clearly as `BLOCKED`; livelock looks like busy, healthy threads.
- **Retry collision**: livelock often comes from conflict-and-retry logic that collides at the same timing.
- **Prevention**: lock ordering prevents deadlock; randomized backoff prevents livelock.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Deadlock and livelock are both ways threads get stuck, but they're completely different in how they behave. In deadlock, threads are blocked and waiting. They're parked, doing absolutely nothing, consuming no CPU. You see them in BLOCKED state in a thread dump. In livelock, threads are actively running code. They're in RUNNABLE state, consuming CPU, executing instructions, but they're not making any actual progress. The classic analogy is two polite people in a hallway. They meet, both step right to let the other pass, and block each other. They both step left, blocking again. They keep switching sides, actively moving but never passing. That's livelock. In code, you see this with optimistic retry logic. Two threads detect a conflict, back off, and retry. But their timing is such that they collide again in the same pattern, over and over. Here's why livelock is harder to detect in production: thread dumps show the threads as RUNNABLE, so your monitoring thinks everything is fine. High CPU usage, threads are busy, but nothing is getting done. With deadlock, you see threads clearly stuck in BLOCKED state. The solution for livelock is usually adding randomized backoff delays so threads don't keep colliding at the same moment.

questions.question: What is memory inconsistency and how does the Java Memory Model address it?
questions.title: Memory Inconsistency and Java Memory Model
questions.direct_answer: Memory inconsistency is when different threads see different values for the same variable due to CPU caches and compiler optimizations. The Java Memory Model defines happens-before rules that specify when one thread's writes are guaranteed to be visible to another thread. Use volatile, synchronized, or concurrent utilities to enforce visibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the JMM conceptually — a strong differentiation point for freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the JMM exists or thinking Java memory is always consistent across threads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the key happens-before rules: program order, monitor lock, volatile, thread start and join

sections.title: Memory Inconsistency and the Java Memory Model
sections.content:
**Memory inconsistency** is when different threads see different values for the same variable, even though there is logically one shared value.

This happens because each CPU core has its own **cache**. When Thread A on Core 1 writes `ready = true`, that write lands in Core 1's cache first. Thread B on Core 2 may still read `ready = false` from its own cache. On top of that, the compiler and JVM can **reorder instructions** for speed, so operations need not run in the order you wrote them.

The **Java Memory Model (JMM)** defines when one thread's write is guaranteed to be visible to another, through **happens-before** relationships.

> **Key rule:** wall-clock order means nothing. Only a happens-before edge — created by `volatile`, `synchronized`, or thread start/join — guarantees visibility.

sections.title: Why a Stale Cache Hides a Write
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB W[Thread A writes value] --> C1[Lives in core 1 cache] C1 --> M[Main memory
not updated yet] R[Thread B reads value] --> C2[Reads core 2 cache] C2 --> St[Sees a stale value] M --> Sync[volatile or synchronized
flushes and refreshes] Sync --> F[Fresh value is seen] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Memory Inconsistency|~Threads see old values|stale cached reads|write not propagated|disagreeing views
blue|Java Memory Model|~The rulebook|defines visibility|happens-before|reordering rules
emerald|happens-before|~Visibility guarantee|volatile write to read|lock release to acquire|start/join
violet|Fixes|~Establish ordering|volatile|synchronized|concurrent utilities

sections.title: Wrong: a non-volatile flag can be cached or reordered
Right: volatile establishes happens-before
When Memory Visibility Matters
sections.content:
Memory visibility matters in any multi-threaded code where one thread writes and another reads shared state without a lock. The classic case is a flag that signals readiness or shutdown — one thread sets `shouldStop = true`, another checks it in a loop. Without `volatile`, the reader may loop forever on a stale value.

Lazy initialization and publisher-subscriber patterns need the same care: readers must see a fully built object, not a half-published one. The double-checked locking singleton requires `volatile` on the instance field. Any shared state changed without `synchronized` must consider visibility.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing the JMM exists**: many freshers think Java handles cross-thread consistency automatically, missing that you need explicit happens-before edges.
- **Assuming writes are instantly visible**: expecting Thread B to see Thread A's write immediately is false without synchronization, because of CPU caches.
- **Forgetting `synchronized` also gives visibility**: it is not only mutual exclusion — all writes before a lock release are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Memory inconsistency**: different threads seeing different values due to CPU caches and instruction reordering.
- **CPU caches**: each core caches values, so a write is not immediately visible to other cores.
- **Java Memory Model**: defines happens-before rules that say when writes become visible across threads.
- **happens-before**: if A happens-before B, then A's effects are visible to B.
- **volatile**: a volatile write is flushed to main memory and visible to all later reads.
- **Key rules**: program order, monitor lock, volatile, thread start, and thread join.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Memory inconsistency is when different threads see different values for the same variable even though logically there's one shared value. This happens because of how modern CPUs work. Each core has its own cache, and when a thread writes to a variable, that write goes to its core's cache first, not immediately to main memory. Another thread on a different core might still see the old value. On top of that, the compiler and JVM can reorder instructions, so operations might not happen in the order you wrote them. The Java Memory Model, or JMM, defines when one thread's writes are guaranteed to be visible to another through happens-before relationships. Here's a concrete example. You have a config-loaded flag. Thread A loads a configuration object and sets the flag to true. Thread B checks the flag, sees it's true, and tries to use the config object. But due to reordering or caching, the config object might still be null in Thread B's view. That's memory inconsistency. The fix is making the flag volatile. The volatile keyword establishes a happens-before relationship. All writes before writing to a volatile variable are visible to all reads after reading it. Synchronized blocks give the same guarantee. The key happens-before rules are program order within a thread, monitor lock acquire and release, volatile reads and writes, thread start, and thread join.

beats.text: Memory inconsistency is when two threads see different values for the same variable. CPU caches and instruction reordering cause it. The Java Memory Model defines happens-before rules. They say exactly when one thread's write is visible to another.

CPUs and JVMs reorder and cache values for speed. Without an ordering rule, timing proves nothing. Thread A might write a value, and Thread B might still read the old one. The write may not have reached main memory yet.

items: Program order: inside one thread, each step happens-before the next.
Monitor lock: a release happens-before the next lock on the same monitor.
Volatile: a volatile write happens-before every later read of it.
Thread start and join: `start` happens-before the new thread's work.

beats.text: Picture a flag set to true at ten o'clock. Another thread reads it a second later. Here's the non-obvious part. The JVM can still return false. Timing alone gives no guarantee. Only `volatile`, `synchronized`, or a thread start creates the real happens-before edge.

items: Syncing the write but not the read still breaks. An unsynced read sees a stale value.
Without `volatile` or `synchronized`, one thread's flag change may never arrive.

speakable_v2.cap: So the Java Memory Model is the contract for visibility. Happens-before is why `volatile` and `synchronized` exist.
